prompt: Match each part of Airflow to what it does.
hint: One of them has to be awake at three in the morning.

pairs.right: works out which tasks are due
holds the state of every run

prompt: In a Composer 3 environment, where do the DAG files go?
hint: It is the one part you can see.

choices.text: On the scheduler's disk, copied with scp
choices.why: The machines are in a project of Google's, out of your sight; you never log in to them.

choices.text: In the dags/ folder of the environment's bucket
choices.why: Right: the bucket is what you see, and the scheduler reads the folder from it.

choices.text: In the Cloud SQL database, as rows
choices.why: The database holds the state of runs, not the files that describe them.

choices.text: In Artifact Registry, as a container image built from the files
choices.why: DAGs are plain Python files in the bucket; nothing is built.

prompt: Python runs quitanda_nightly.py from top to bottom. What has happened when it finishes?
hint: A DAG file is a description.

choices.text: The four commands ran, once each, in the order of the arrows
choices.why: Nothing ran: the file only creates operators and arrows for the scheduler to read.

choices.text: A DAG of four tasks and three arrows, and nothing has run at all
choices.why: Right: runs and task instances are created later, by the scheduler or by dags test.

choices.text: A run for today was queued
choices.why: Queuing runs is the scheduler's job, and a new DAG starts paused.

choices.text: {DAY} was replaced by yesterday's date
choices.why: Templates are rendered per run, when a task runs.

prompt: On Composer, the export_orders task becomes a GCSObjectExistenceSensor. What does that change about when the pipeline starts working?
hint: What does a sensor wait for?

choices.text: It waits for the night's file
choices.why: Right: the sensor checks for the night's object until it appears.

choices.text: Nothing, because the schedule alone decides when every task starts
choices.why: The schedule creates the run; the sensor then holds the next task until the file exists.

choices.text: It writes the export itself
choices.why: A sensor only checks; the shop writes the export.

choices.text: It starts the Spark job sooner
choices.why: It can only make it later, never sooner than the file.

prompt: The environment variable for the `load_examples` option of the `[core]` section of airflow.cfg is ___.
hint: Two underscores on each side of the section.

prompt: Why does the lesson put the Airflow environment at the END of PATH, after the course's?
hint: Which python3 does a task get?

choices.text: So that python3 and spark-submit in a task are still lesson 23's
choices.why: Right: only airflow itself comes from the second environment.

choices.text: Because Airflow refuses to start when its environment comes first on the path
choices.why: Airflow does not look at its place on the path.

choices.text: To make the course's duckdb visible to the scheduler
choices.why: The scheduler does not import duckdb; the tasks' commands do, through python3.

choices.text: To keep the constraints file from being read twice
choices.why: The constraints file is read once, by pip, at install time.

prompt: A DAG file has just been copied into the DAG folder. Why will the scheduler not run it on its own?
hint: Look at the column dags list printed.

choices.text: It needs dags test first
choices.why: dags test is a way to run it by hand, not a precondition.

choices.text: It is paused
choices.why: Right: is_paused True, until somebody unpauses it.

choices.text: catchup=False stops all scheduling of a new DAG
choices.why: catchup=False only limits a late start to the latest run.

choices.text: The start date is in the future
choices.why: It is 26 October, before the capture was made.

prompt: A team wants Composer to cost nothing over a month when no pipeline runs. What can it do?
hint: Is there a stopped state?

choices.text: Pause the environment
choices.why: An environment has no paused state; pausing a DAG stops runs, not the bill.

choices.text: Set the workers to zero
choices.why: The scheduler, the database and the infrastructure keep billing, and at least one worker stays.

choices.text: Save a snapshot and delete the environment, then recreate it later
choices.why: Right: deleting is the only way to stop paying, and a snapshot is how the history survives it.

choices.text: Switch it to Composer 2, which bills only for the hours tasks are running
choices.why: Composer 2 bills an environment fee every hour, 0.56 for a small one in São Paulo.

prompt: A small Composer 2 environment costs 523.85 USD a month idle. Twenty-five DAGs share it. What does each DAG cost a month, in USD, to two decimals?
hint: The environment divided by the DAGs.

prompt: Why does the lesson price Composer 3 at 12 DCUs, while it prices Composer 2 from a list of components?
hint: What does each part of the page say?

choices.text: Because 12 DCUs is the minimum Composer 3 allows
choices.why: The page states no minimum; 12 is its worked example.

choices.text: Because only Composer 2's small preset is listed on the page, item by item
choices.why: Right: an idle Composer 3 environment's DCUs are not on the page, so the example is used and labelled.

choices.text: Because Composer 3 bills in milli DCUs, which cannot be converted
choices.why: A thousand milli DCU-hours is one DCU-hour; the program converts it in a comment.

choices.text: Because the two generations cost the same
choices.why: The program printed 838.41 and 523.85.

prompt: A Cloud Scheduler job is created with --schedule='0 3 * * *' and no --time-zone. When does it fire in São Paulo?
hint: The help printed the default.

choices.why: That needs --time-zone=America/Sao_Paulo.
06:00 UTC is three in the morning in São Paulo: that is the conversion done the other way round.

choices.text: At midnight
choices.why: Right: the default is Etc/UTC, and 03:00 UTC is midnight in São Paulo.

choices.text: It is refused without a time zone
choices.why: The flag has a default, so the job is accepted.

prompt: On the 3rd, somebody re-runs the workflow by hand to redo the night of the 1st. What does it process?
hint: Where does pick_day get its date?

choices.text: The 1st, because the execution remembers its schedule
choices.why: A workflow knows only when it runs; it has no logical date.

choices.text: The 2nd, the day before the moment it runs
choices.why: Right: sys.now() less a day, which is why a past night needs the day passed in.

choices.text: The 3rd, the day it runs
choices.why: pick_day subtracts a day's seconds first.

choices.text: Nothing: a workflow refuses to run outside its schedule
choices.why: A workflow runs whenever an execution is started; Scheduler is only one way to start one.

prompt: Which of these does the lesson say Workflows with Cloud Scheduler lacks, compared with Composer? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read the table at the end of the section.

choices.text: A backfill command for a range of days
choices.why: Yes: a past day is an execution started by hand.

choices.text: A data interval for each run
choices.why: Yes: the workflow takes its day from the clock.

choices.text: A way to call the Dataproc API
choices.why: The workflow calls it through a connector and waits for the batch.

choices.text: A schedule in the five-field cron form
choices.why: Cloud Scheduler uses the same five-field form as the DAG.

prompt: In Airflow 3, a DAG with schedule='0 3 * * *' runs at 03:00 on the 30th. What is its ds?
hint: Which timetable does a cron string mean in Airflow 3?

choices.text: 2026-10-29, the day that has just ended
choices.why: That is CronDataIntervalTimetable, Airflow 2's reading of the same string.

choices.text: 2026-10-30, the night it runs
choices.why: Right: CronTriggerTimetable gives the run the moment it fires, which is why the DAG says ds_add(ds, -1).

choices.text: 2026-10-31, the start of the next interval
choices.why: Nothing in either timetable looks forward to the 31st.

choices.text: It depends on when the task finishes
choices.why: ds is fixed when the run is created, whenever its tasks end.

prompt: A clock_interval DAG starts on the 26th with catchup=True, and the scheduler first reads it at 19:00 on the 30th. How many runs does it create?
hint: A run starts when its day ends.

prompt: A backfill is wanted for the nights of the 20th to the 23rd, inclusive. Why did --to-date 2026-10-23 return only three runs?
hint: What moment does a date name?

choices.text: Backfill skips the newest date on purpose
choices.why: It includes the end of the range; the range simply ended too early.

choices.text: The 23rd had already run, and --reprocess-behavior was left at none
choices.why: No run for the 23rd existed; the dry run listed none.

choices.text: The date means midnight UTC, six hours before that night's 06:00 UTC run
choices.why: Right: the run of the 23rd is at 06:00 UTC, past the end of the range.

choices.text: --dry-run lists at most three runs
choices.why: The dry run lists every run the backfill would create.

prompt: A DAG written for Airflow 2 uses {{ ds }} as "yesterday" and is moved unchanged to Airflow 3 with the same cron string. What goes wrong?
hint: Compare the two timelines of the figure.

choices.text: It fails to parse, because ds was removed
choices.why: ds exists in Airflow 3; what changed is which date it holds.

choices.text: It processes a day that has barely begun
choices.why: Right: on the trigger timetable ds is the night of the run, three hours old.

choices.text: It runs twice a night, once per timetable
choices.why: A DAG has one timetable; the string now means a different one.

choices.text: Nothing, since Airflow 3 converts the old DAGs as it reads them
choices.why: No conversion happens; the same string is simply read differently.

prompt: Order the monthly orchestration cost for Quitanda's one pipeline, cheapest first, as the program printed it.
hint: One of them is inside the free allowances.

prompt: Three teams, thirty DAGs that depend on each other, and a habit of re-running last week. Which choice does the lesson favour?
hint: What does each option do with "the run for the 22nd"?

choices.text: Workflows, because it costs nothing between runs
choices.why: True of the bill, and every re-run would be an execution started by hand with its day passed in.

choices.text: Composer, whose idle bill is shared by thirty DAGs
choices.why: Right: backfills, dependencies and history are Airflow's, and 523.85 shared thirty ways is about 17 a DAG.

choices.text: Cloud Scheduler alone, with one job for each of the thirty DAGs
choices.why: Scheduler starts things; it has no dependencies, retries or history of the work.

choices.text: Airflow on a laptop, as in the lab
choices.why: Nothing keeps running there once the terminal closes.

prompt: Why does the lesson have each step take its date as an argument, as daily_orders.py takes --dt?
hint: What changes when a team moves from Workflows to Composer?

choices.text: Spark refuses to read a partition without it
choices.why: Spark reads whatever path it is given; the argument is about who decides the date.

choices.text: So only what starts the jobs changes
choices.why: Right: the jobs stay, and Airflow or a workflow passes them the day.

choices.text: It makes the jobs cheaper to run
choices.why: The cost of a job is its machines and hours; the argument changes neither.

choices.text: Composer requires every task to take --dt
choices.why: Composer requires nothing of the commands a task runs.
